extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical natural philosophy, aesthetics, musicology, horticulture, and practical arts (cookery/viticulture)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for judging or producing sensory phenomena (sight, sound, smell, taste) and related practical arts (music, painting, grafting, wine/pickle preservation) as presented in a classical treatise on the senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and symmetry (proportione & symmetria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulchritudo (beauty) is apprehended by the eye when parts stand in determinate proportion (e.g. double, triple, quadruple, sesquialtera, sequi-), and when symmetry (aequalitas) is present in arranged elements (columns, trees, faces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: human face, columns, trees — the eye recognizes beauty via simple numeric proportions (dupla, tripla, quadrupla, sesquialtera, sequi-). Vitruvian advice: reduce architectural measures to proportions perceptible to the eye. Lack of proportion is judged ugly or coarse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive recognizability / intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Delectatio in cognoscendo: pleasure arises when the sensible is known and determinate rather than infinite, confused, or indeterminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is obscure or indeterminate cannot delight; intelligibility and the ability to grasp proportions produce delight. Thus artworks or objects should present recognizable, determinate forms to be pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity, nobility, variety, and novelty as contributors to delight
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobilitas, raritas, varietas & permutatio increase attraction; we love what is rare, noble, or novel because it is less easily obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbidden or difficult-to-attain objects excite stronger desire. Variety and permutation prevent satiety; deliberate variety is a source of pleasure in the visual and other senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate specific bodily features (facial attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain physical traits contribute to perceived beauty: smooth skin (cutis glabra), rosy color (roseus color), visible and properly formed teeth (acieu dent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers often love on first sight; features like evenness of skin, healthy color, and pleasant dental appearance are singled out as direct contributors to facial beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination and habituation amplify attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Amor (love/attraction) is strengthened when the imagination forms and repeats the beautiful form; practice/exercise of the imaginative faculty increases attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects retained in the imaginativa prompt stronger love; study and repeated attention intensify desire and impede higher (more spiritual) operations of the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three common conditions of all sensibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Sunt porro communes omnium sensibilium conditiones, tres: (1) proportion (proportione), (2) moderation (quod moderata omnia placent), (3) that better things please after the worse (contrast/relief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Proportion/ratio is primary for delight. 2) Moderation prevents fatigue or offense (extreme loudness, sharpness, etc. displeases). 3) Contrast (improvement after a worse state) enhances pleasure — e.g., sweetness after bitterness, light after darkness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical interval proportions that please (diapason, diapente, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure in musical sound depends on simple numerical proportions: diapason (double), diapente (triple), diatessaron/other intervals follow fixed multiplicative relations (diapason dupla, diapente tripla, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise enumerates ratios (diapason double, diapente triple, subsequent intervals like fefquitertia, semitonium relationships) and asserts that near-integer proportional relations produce consonance and delectation. Simpler integral ratios are more pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in sound (volume/tempo) — 'Secundaratio'
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation: sounds that are moderate in degree (not too great nor too small, not too fast nor too slow) please the ear; extremes fatigue or offend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too loud or too rapid motions weary and annoy; too soft or rare sounds lead to different affects (compassion, relaxation). Balance tempo and loudness to intended affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and timbral quality influence affect (acute/grave/medium; soft/rough)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounds differ by pitch (acutus, gravis, medius), velocity (celer/vel tardo), and timbre (mollis, asper); these properties move different passions: harsh (asper) and quick (celer) provoke excitement/anger; soft/rare induce compassion or calm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select pitch, articulation, and texture to elicit intended emotion; e.g., rough/harsh sounds incite anger/pride; soft/modal sounds induce compassion or relaxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance vs dissonance and perceptual threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Consonance (harmonia) is perceived as ratioical multi-voice order; if component differences are too minute they may fail perception, producing neither delight nor offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If intervals or pictorial details are cut so minute that sense cannot perceive them, they neither delight nor offend; artists/composers should keep perceptible differences so that delights register without producing dissonant offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale-sensitivity and detectability across senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Senses differ in resolving power and scale-sensitivity: some errors are more evident in large works than in small; hearing detects subtler differences in pitch than vision detects small pictorial variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale errors in painting or sculpture are readily perceived and offend; very small errors may go unnoticed. Use this to judge level of finish/detail appropriate to medium and viewing conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of instruments/timbres to move particular affects
rubrics_metrics.description: Different instruments and timbres are fit to evoke specific passions (lyre, cithara, hydrau-lica, cornu, organa etc. produce different effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose instrument and registration according to the intended effect: some instruments (trumpet-like) rouse soldiers; lyre arouses modest pleasure or chastity; organ/hydraulics can be wondrous and overwhelming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Odor's moral/physiological power (odor can revive or kill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Odor has noble power: ‘solus odor ... aut occidere, aut recreare hominem potest’ — a good odor can revive the spirit and is even taken as a divine omen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design/choose odors that either restore or refresh the spirit; good smells are associated with divine favor and health, bad smells with decay and disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Olfactory sensitivity linked to temperament and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Those with warm and dry cerebral temperament are more acute at smelling and more prompt in imagination; olfactory acuity varies by constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for individual differences in olfactory sensitivity when composing perfumes or diagnosing effects; strong imaginations accompany greater olfactory responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste/odor combination and culinary/preservation principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Flavour and smell are closely allied; adding acids, spices, salts, vinegar, and heat alters odor/flavor and can preserve food or mask spoilage (e.g., use of vinegar, pepper, mustard, cinnamon, pitch-lined vessels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules: use acids and sharp spices to prevent putrefaction or mask bad smells; add honey/other sweet parts to fermented must to change outcome; choose appropriate vessel treatment (pitch, resin) and storage temperature to preserve figs, wines, and fruits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wine and must preservation (methods and vessel treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent wine turning to vinegar and to preserve must: seal vessels well, use pitch/coating, pick good vessel material, sometimes immerse vessels in running water for a month; temperature control and packing methods matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical recipes given: pitch-lined amphorae, repeated heating/cooling steps, addition of aromatic/herbal substances (hyssop, nard, crocus, aloes), keeping vessels in river for a month, and avoiding exposure that causes separation and exhalation of volatile sweet parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spices and acidification to create desired tastes/odours (pickling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain fruits and meats are made pleasant and preserved by treatment with strong vinegar, salt, spices (pepper, mustard, cinnamon), or fermentation; different woods impart different effects when used for smoking/pickling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical combinations: use sharp vinegar/acid for pickling (pyra, corna), mix with aromatic herbs for flavour and preservation; heating and controlled drying influence the final odour and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grafting/infusion rules for altering plant fruit properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Grafting (infito/insitio) can change fruit color, flavor, and other qualities; success depends on grafting durable parts (medulla), suitable stock, and time for the graft to become established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To change fruit color/flavor effectively, graft using parts that carry the desired sap (often medulla), and prefer long-lasting, strong unions; transient or weak grafts will not transmit traits. Examples: changing morus color by inserting citrion etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of plant environment to alter phenology (flowering/fruiting)
rubrics_metrics.description: To have flowers or fruits out of season or to hasten maturity, keep plants in warmer, sheltered places, use vessels/containers, or physically manipulate branches (e.g., include in pots, expose to sun), and manage humidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical techniques: keep plants in warm locations, cover/contain them, use cuttings stored in warm conditions, and manage moisture and shade to induce early or prolonged flowering/fruiting.
